extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of dramatic theory (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragic plays: how to construct plots, recognitions, reversals, characters, and parts of tragedy so as to produce the proper tragic effect (pity and fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of the Situation (Peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject always to our rule of probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal should arise naturally from the plot (not arbitrarily). Examples: in Oedipus the messenger comes to cheer but by revealing who he is produces the opposite effect; in Lynceus, Danaus intends to kill Lynceus but is killed himself. Reversal is most effective when coincident with recognition and when it follows from probable or necessary sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between the persons destined by the poet for good or bad fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best when coincident with reversal (produces pity or fear). Recognition most intimately connected with plot is recognition of persons, though objects or proofs may be used. Several kinds exist (signs, tokens, memory, reasoning, poet-invented), and recognitions that arise naturally from incidents are best; artificial or poet-inserted recognitions are less artistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene of Suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: A destructive or painful action, such as death on the stage, bodily agony, wounds and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes of suffering are elements of tragedy that can produce pity and fear; handle them with attention to their place within the plot and to how they arise from character and incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative Parts of Tragedy (structural units)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into Prologue, Episode, Exode, Choric song (Parode and Stasimon); some plays have stage-songs (songs of actors) and Commos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: Prologue precedes the Parode of the Chorus; Episode is between complete choric songs; Exode has no choric song after it; Parode is chorus' first utterance; Stasimon is a choric ode without anapaests or trochaic tetrameters; Commos is joint lamentation of Chorus and actors. These units should be used appropriately when constructing a play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should be complex (involving Reversal and Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect tragedy should be arranged not on the simple but on the complex plan, and should imitate actions which excite pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots (with reversal and recognition) create the distinctive tragic effect. The complication and its unraveling should arise from the plot itself rather than external contrivances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic effect must be pity and fear (defining aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should imitate actions which excite pity and fear; this is the distinctive mark of tragic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet's pleasure to produce is the emotional response of pity and fear through imitation (not merely spectacle). Choose incidents and relations that naturally arouse these emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper type of protagonist (middling stature with error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not a virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity (moves neither pity nor fear), nor an utter villain; rather a man who is not eminently good and just, yet whose misfortune is brought about not by vice but by some error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protagonists should be notable/renowned but flawed by an error (hamartia) that plausibly produces their downfall (examples: Oedipus, Thyestes). This evokes pity (unmerited misfortune) and fear (a man-like ourselves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of fortune should be from good to bad and arise from error
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune should be not from bad to good but, reversely, from good to bad; it should come about as the result not of vice but of some great error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plots that merely shock (virtue->misfortune without pity/fear), or satisfy only moral sense (villain downfall). The causal link between character error and catastrophe must be clear and probable/necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plot (single issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well constructed plot should be single in its issue, rather than double.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid divided or double catastrophes when aiming for true tragic effect; single focused issue yields stronger tragic impact (though double-thread plots may please weaker audiences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use traditional subject-matter skilfully (few houses/families)
rubrics_metrics.description: Best tragedies are founded on the story of a few houses; poets are compelled to have recourse to those houses whose history contains moving incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not destroy traditional frameworks but show invention and skillfully handle received legends—present traditional material with fresh, artful treatment rather than mere repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer inner structure over spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means; but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is the better way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to produce the tragic effect through plot and incident so the tale thrills when heard alone. Reliance on spectacle risks producing the monstrous rather than the tragic; spectacle is secondary and potentially extraneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select relations that maximize pity/fear (kinship and intimacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of tragic effect must happen between persons who are friends or enemies or indifferent; pity/fear are especially aroused when incidents occur between those who are near or dear (kin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek incidents among close relatives (brother killing brother, son and father, mother and son, etc.) to heighten emotional stakes. If traditional legends fix who kills whom, inventiveness should be in handling, not necessarily in altering the framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering of horrific deeds and discovery (ranked methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deed must either be done or not done, and that wittingly or unwittingly; the best way is that the deed should be perpetrated in ignorance and the discovery made afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranking: worst — about to act knowing the persons then not to act (shocking without being tragic); better — deed perpetrated; best — deed perpetrated in ignorance with discovery after (startling effect without gratuitous shock). Use these orderings to structure scenes of horror for maximal tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: four aims (goodness, propriety, verisimilitude, consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of Character there are four things to be aimed at: (1) goodness, (2) propriety, (3) true-to-life, (4) consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Goodness: speech/action that manifests moral purpose marks character as good (relative to class). 2) Propriety: traits appropriate to class/sex/status (avoid inappropriate valor in a woman as a general characteristic). 3) True-to-life (verisimilitude) distinct from moral goodness. 4) Consistency: even if source is inconsistent, portrayal must be consistently inconsistent; avoid motiveless degradations or sudden inappropriate shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character actions must follow necessity or probability
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of a given character should speak or act in a given way, by the rule either of necessity or of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the complication and unraveling of the plot must arise from characters and incidents by necessary or probable sequence; avoid arbitrary actions that break verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Deus ex Machina inside the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The unravelling must arise out of the plot itself, it must not be brought about by the Deus ex Machina; the Deus ex Machina should be employed only for events external to the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve internal dramatic problems by divine contrivance; such devices are acceptable only for antecedent or subsequent events beyond human knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition types and their ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinds of recognition: (1) by signs (congenital or acquired tokens), (2) by tokens/formal proof (less artistic), (3) by a turn of incident, (4) recognitions invented by the poet (bad), (5) by memory (sight/hearing awakens feeling), (6) by process of reasoning, (7) composite involving false inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best recognitions arise naturally from incidents (e.g., Oedipus, Iphigenia). Next best are recognitions by reasoning. Least artistic are contrived tokens or poet-inserted revelations (e.g., a character simply stating who he is). Avoid recognitions that feel invented solely for proof or convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose scenes visually and work out stage coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing the plot and working it out with proper diction, the poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualizing the action like a spectator helps discover inconsistencies and avoid stage oversights (example: failure in Carcinus where Amphiaraus' movement was overlooked). Work out appropriate gestures and stage business to maintain credibility and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should ennoble types while preserving likeness to life
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Tragedy is an imitation of persons who are above the common level, the poet should, while reproducing the distinctive form of the original, make a likeness which is true to life and yet more beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray defects (irascibility, indolence) but ennoble the character (idealize) so the portrait is true to type yet elevated (like a good portrait-painter). This enhances tragic dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensory appeals and gestures as concomitants, not essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the senses (spectacle, music, gesture) are not among the essentials but are concomitants of poetry and admit of much room for error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not neglect sensory elements, but treat them as secondary supports to the essential plot/character structure. Overreliance or misuse can spoil the tragic effect.
